topic: What if you had infinite money?
title: WHAT IF YOU HAD
INFINITE MONEY?

power.rule: a black card with no limit, real money, never runs out
power.look: card chip BALANCE: ∞, terminal beep, green PAYMENT APPROVED

script.text: A black card. No spending limit.
Buy every sandwich on the whole street. Tap. Payment approved.
Buy an entire island. Tap. Payment approved.
What if you had infinite money?
This morning, there's an envelope in your mailbox with no name on it. Inside is a black card, and a note with just two words: no limit.
Buy anything. As much as you want. The bank has checked it: it's real money, and it never runs out.
You try buying a bubble tea. Tap. Payment approved. Your balance comes up: infinity.

To give you a sense of scale: in twenty twenty five, Vietnam's entire economy produced about five hundred billion dollars' worth of goods and services. With this card, one tap covers all of it. Then you tap again.
On day one, you buy breakfast for the whole neighborhood. Sandwiches, noodle soup, sticky rice, coffee. Tap.
You pay off your parents' mortgage. You buy your little sister an entire toy store. You give your best friend a brand new scooter. Tap, tap, tap.
You rebuild your old school. Cool classrooms, a library full of books, a brand new football pitch. You open a movie theater and let the whole school in for free.
You buy the tallest building in the city, and open the rooftop so anyone can watch the sunset for free. You buy a trip to space. Tickets cost tens of millions of dollars. Tap.
Then you think bigger. According to a study called Ceres twenty thirty, the world needs about thirty three billion extra dollars a year to end hunger by twenty thirty. For you, that's one tap.
Sounds like you just became the kindest person on the planet, right? But this card has a problem nobody told you about.
Every time you tap, new money flows into the economy. But not a single new thing gets made.
You buy every sandwich on the street. The next morning, nobody else can buy one. Sellers see that everyone wants to buy, so they raise their prices.
You buy ten thousand bags of rice for flood victims. But farmers can't grow rice as fast as you can tap. Rice runs short. The price goes up, for everyone.
Shopkeepers start to recognize you. When they see you coming, they quietly change their price boards.

This has really happened. In nineteen eighty six, inflation in Vietnam hit seven hundred seventy four point seven percent. Something that cost one dong in January cost almost nine by December. People carried bags of cash to the market. That's real.
In Zimbabwe, at one point prices were doubling about every day. In two thousand nine, the country printed a one hundred trillion dollar note.
And the people who lose the most are the ones who did nothing at all. Your grandma saved her whole life into one savings book. Every time you tap, that book buys a little less.
A week later, a man in a suit comes to see you. He works at the central bank. He says just one thing: please, stop tapping.

That's when you finally understand. Money has no value by itself. Money is just a promise that someone will trade you their work. The rice a farmer grows. A surgeon's operation. The bread a baker gets up at four in the morning to bake.
Infinite money can't make more rice. It can't make more doctors. It can't add a single hour to the day.

The next morning, your mom still gets up early and pushes her sticky rice cart to the end of the alley, like every day. You ask: I have infinite money now, why are you still selling? She smiles: because people still need breakfast, sweetheart.
That day, you help her sell for one morning. For the first time in your life, you hold money you earned yourself. Fifteen thousand dong. It feels heavier than the black card.

So if you had infinite money, what's the smartest way to spend it? Not on more stuff. On helping the world make more things. Build schools to train more doctors. Fund research on better rice. Send poor kids to school.
You pay teachers and doctors in remote villages really well. You fund scientists, so they can find cheaper power and cleaner water.
You tap slower. Less often. But every time you tap, the world gets one more real thing.
A year later, the black card is still in your wallet. You use it less than you ever imagined. And your mom still sells sticky rice at the end of the alley. It's still the best in town.
One day, your best friend asks: if you could choose again, would you still want that card? You think for a long time. Then you say: yes. But now I know what to use it for.
So, if you had a card with no limit, what's the first thing you'd buy? And would you dare to use it to change the world? Tell us in the comments.

science.claim: In 2025 Vietnam's economy produced about $500 billion of goods and services.
science.working: GDP 2025 at current prices: 12,847.6 trillion VND ≈ US$514 billion.
science.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam (NSO), 2025 socio-economic report (Jan 2026)

science.claim: Ceres2030: about $33 billion extra a year to end hunger by 2030.
science.working: Ceres2030 (Cornell, IFPRI, IISD, 2020): ~$330 billion extra to 2030 ≈ $33 billion/year; other estimates are higher, hence 'according to a study'.

science.claim: Space trips cost tens of millions of dollars.
science.working: Private seats to the ISS were reported at about $55 million (2022).

science.claim: New money without new goods raises prices; savers lose.
In 1986 inflation in Vietnam hit 774.7%; 1 dong in January ≈ almost 9 by December.
science.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam; VnExpress

science.claim: Zimbabwe: prices doubled about every day; a 100 trillion dollar note in 2009.
science.working: Hanke & Kwok (2009): peak monthly inflation Nov 2008 79.6 billion %, prices doubling every ~24.7 h; Z$100 trillion note issued Jan 2009.
science.source: S. Hanke & A. Kwok, Cato Journal 29(2), 2009
